title: Coaching Cut 52: Hypothetical Modelling
author: Cognitive Coaching
summary: Cognitive Coaching's 52nd instalment identifies 'hypothetical modelling' as a coaching pitfall: the tendency to describe what a technique looks like in the abstract rather than demonstrate it in practice. The pitfall is seductive because describing sounds like teaching -- both coach and coachee feel knowledge is being transferred. But the gap between understanding a description and being able to perform the behaviour is precisely what modelling is supposed to close. The article distinguishes two levels: level one is describing the behaviour (telling the coachee what to do); level two is performing the behaviour in the coaching conversation itself (showing the coachee in real time what it looks like). Hypothetical modelling stops at level one. The coachee leaves with a concept but no felt sense of the behaviour's texture, timing, or social feel. The author argues that coaches default to hypothetical modelling not from laziness but from a reluctance to be evaluated. Demonstrating a technique in the moment exposes the coach to feedback; describing it does not. This makes hypothetical modelling a subtle form of self-protection masquerading as instruction. The fix is deliberate: the next time you are about to say 'for example, you could say something like...' pause and say 'let me actually try that with you right now.' The discomfort of real-time modelling is the signal that learning is happening on both sides of the conversation.
points: Hypothetical modelling -- describing what a technique looks like rather than demonstrating it -- creates the illusion of skill transfer while leaving the coachee without the felt sense of timing, tone, and texture that determines whether they can actually use the technique.
Description builds propositional knowledge; demonstration builds procedural knowledge -- only the latter transfers to new performance contexts.

Coaches who default to hypothetical modelling often do so as a form of self-protection: describing a technique cannot be evaluated, while demonstrating it can -- structurally identical to the reluctance they are trying to help the coachee overcome.

The practical test: if the phrase 'you could say something like' appears in your coaching followed by an indirect paraphrase rather than a direct utterance, you have described rather than demonstrated.

Real-time modelling is generative for the coach as well: performing a technique rather than describing it reveals whether the coach can actually do it -- often more instructive than the coaching session itself.
quotes: Pitfall: Describing rather than demonstrating. The coach explains what a good question looks like rather than asking one. The coachee understands the concept. They leave unable to use it.

There are two things you can do when a coachee needs to see a new behaviour. You can describe it -- tell them what it looks like, how it works, what it sounds like in the abstract. Or you can do it, right there in the session, and let them feel it from the inside. Only the second one counts as modelling.

The signal that you are hypothetically modelling is the phrase 'for example, you might say something like.' This construction allows the coach to gesture toward a behaviour without committing to performing it. It sounds instructive. It teaches very little.

Every coach has a self-protective instinct to describe rather than demonstrate. Description cannot be evaluated. The coachee cannot say 'that didn't quite work' about something you only described. Demonstration exposes you. That exposure is the mechanism of modelling.

When a coach models a technique in real time, they discover whether they can actually do it. Frequently, they discover they cannot -- that their description of the technique was more polished than their execution of it. This is more valuable than the coachee's learning.
